Dated Calcutta, the 22nd November 1960. 


Whereas | am satisfied that in view of the 
serious congestion which is causing difficulty in 
the circulation of vehicular trafic on Balmukund 
(Mackar Roud between Chitturanjan Avenue and 
Madan Mohan Burman Street due ہا‎ the 
obstruction caused by the parking ot goods vehicles 
oud heavy transport vehicles, it is mnecesary to 
restrict the parking, loading or unloading of the 
1119, of the motor vehicles mentioned above on 
that road between the hours only of 6 a.m. and 
8 p.m. on all days, in the interest of the general 
public convenience, in exercise of the powers 
vested in me by sections 75 and 76 of the Motor 
Vehicles Act, 1939 (Act 1٦ of 1939), read with 
Government of West Bengal, Home (Transport) 
Department, order No, 24683W.T., dated the 9th 
April 1957, 1 hereby make the following order :— 


Goods vehicles commonly called ‘lorries’? and 
heavy transport vehicles and chassis of the 
abovementioned types of motor vehicles, 
trailers und tractors shall not park, load or 
unload goods on the north side of Bal- 
mukund Mackar Road between the hours 
only of 6 a.m. and 8 p.m. on all days.

470 that an agreement or scttlement which is not

the Calcutta Improvement Act, 1911 (as 
amended), that the Board of Trustees for the 
Improvement of Calcutta have applied to the 
State Government for sanction to the Improve- 
ment Scheme No. LXVI (Blackburn Lane to 
Lower Chitpur Road) as revised, which was first 
published in the ‘‘Calcutta Gazette” and in 1008] 
newspapers on 28th April 1960. 


Dated Calcutta, the llth November 1960. 


Notice is hereby given under section 63(5) of 
the Calcutta mprovement Act, 191], as 
amended, that the Board of Trustees for the 
Improvement of Calcutta have applied to the 
State Government for sanction to the plan of the 
proposed Public Street No. VIII (Cossipore— 
from Ranee Harshamukhi Road to Dum Dum

the ‘Calcutta Gazette” and in local newspapers 
on the 3rd September 1959.

(000৭ the present dearness allowance is 0

ay alleged by the Union and has finally contended

weak financial position of the Company. The 
Company has also supported its case by the further 
৪1910116171 that the emplovees are also being paid 
bonus and some special allowances in addition to 
the ordinary allowances as per the statement in 
this behalf annexed to its written statement and 
marked “B’’, The substance of the Company's 
case 11) regard to the Union’s claim is, therefore, 
that the total emoluments of the employees 
including ordinary alowance, bonus and special 
allowance as these stand nat present are not 
insufficient to meet their ordinary cost of living 
and in any case, the present financial position of 
{he Company does not warrant any further increase 
in the emoluments of its staff and the Company is 
not capable of being saddled with any = further 
habilitv in regard to the emoluments pnyable to 
119 staff. It ia further the Company's ۱۸۸۸ء‎ that its

in view of this position and the uneconomic position

oharges’’.

G.S.R. 1410.—In exercise of the powers conferred by section 3 of the 
11889871619] Commodities Act, 1955 (10 of 1955), the Central Government 
hereby makes the following Order to amend the Rice (Eastern Zone) 
Movement Control Ordor, 1959, namely :— 

1. This Order may be called the Rice (Eastern Zone) Movement Control 
(Third Amendment) Order, 1960.

clause 4, the following clause shall be inserted, namely :—

border area in the course of export to any place within such 


territory.

17000107040 notes.—Regarding the amendments made, the

No. 14086 | M.8E-43/58.—8th December 1960. 
—Whereas the Commissioners of the Bhatpara 
Municipality in the district of 24-Parganas have, 
with the approval of the State Government, made 
the following rule under sub-section (1) of section 
69 of the Bengal Municipal Act, 1982 (Bengal Act 
XV of 1982), and have apphed to the State Govern- 
ment for confirmation of the said rule under section 
800 of the said Act; 


And whereas— 


(a) notice of the intention to apply for such 
confirmation of the said rule has been 
duly given one month before the making 
of the application for confirmation as 
required under clause (i) of sub-section 
(2) of section 506 of the said Act; and 


(b) for one month before the making of the 
application a copy of the said rule has 
been kept at the office of the Commissioners 
of the said municipality, and has been 
opened during office hours therent to the 
inspection of the inhabitants of the said 
municipality, without fee, na required by 
clause (ii) of sub-section (2) of section 
2006) of the said Act; 


Now. therefore. in exercise of the power 
conferred by section 506 of the Bengal Municipal 
Act, 1932 (Bengal Act XV of 1932), the Governor 
is pleased to confirm the following rule, namely :— 


Crant of compassionate gratuity. 


If an employee is disabled, crippled or killed in 
the courses of his employment or suffers premature 
death during the period of his service under the 
municipality, the Commissioners at a meeting 
may, if they so desire, grant him or his heir or 
next of kin/the members of his family, as the 


3884 THF CALCUTTA GAZETTE, DECEMBER 1 190 
১০১০১১১১০১১ 


cause may be, a compassionate gratuity on the 
following scale: provided that the compassionate 
gratuity shall not be granted to those employees or 
10 their heir or next of ‘kin/the members of their 
families to whom Workmen’s Compensation Act, 
1932, applies and who claim compensation under 
that Act :— 


Scale. 


(1) If the employee is permanently disabled— 
A gratuity not exceeding 24 months’ pay, 


(ii) If the employee sustains partial disable- 
ment rendering him unfit for reversion to 
his former occupation and for whom no 
other suitable employment can be found— 
A gratuity not exceeding 12 months’ pay. 


(111) In the case of an heir or next of kin/the 
membors of the family of an employee, 
killed or dying of injuries received—A 
gratuity not exceeding 24 months’ pay of 
the employee. 


(iv) If the employee suffers premature death, 
rendering satisfactory services to the 
municipality for less than 15 years—A 
gratuity not exceeding half-a-month’s 
pay for each completed year of service. 


The gratuity admissible shall in every case be 
aubject to a maximum of rupees two thousand only. 


Note.—For the purposes of this rule ‘“‘pay”’ 
means— 

(1) the average monthly pay carned by the 

employee during the last 12 months of 

his service if his service be not less than 


12 months, and 


(1i) the average monthly pay earned by the 
employee during the whole service if it is 
less than 12 months, 


By order of the Governor, 
A. N. MUKHERJEE, Asst. Secy.

AWARD 


The above industrial dispute relating to the 
question whether the service rendered by the 14 
workmen, named in the issue piven in the Schedule 
fo the order of reference, prior to lst July 1956 
should count for retrenchment compensation was 
first. referred for adjudication to the First Labour 
Court by the Government of West Bengal, Labour 
Department, order No, 1199-1.2./TR/15L-19/57, 
dated the 24th March 1958, and the same dispute 
has subsequently been referred to this Tribunal 
fer adjudication in supersession of the said previous 
order of reference and after the abolition of the 
anid Firat Labour Court by the Government of 
West Bengal, Dabour Department, — order 
No, 3994-1. RB, /IR/161-19/57, dated the 29) July 


1960. The only issue g ven in the schedule to the 
order of reference stands thus: — 


Whether the serviecs rendered by the following 
workmen prior to Ist July 1956 should 
count for retrenchment compensation. To 
what relief are they entitled ? 


(1) Shri Sambhu Mallick, (ii) Shri Bankim 
Chandra Nath, (iii) Shr: Bhusan 
Chandra Sce, (iv) Shri Dhbirendra 
Nath Mirdey, (v) Shri Radharaman 
Sadhukhan, (vi) Shri Sidheawar 
Barik, (vii) Shri Hari Charan Jana, 
(viii) Shri Kanai Nath Nath, (ix) 
Shri Akshay Kumor_ Paul, (x) Shri 
Ajodhya JBorai, (x!) Shri Bhanu 
Singh, (xii) Shri Subar Kahar, (x1) 
Shri Sahadeo Tohar and (xiv) Shri 
Biswanath Roy. 


After receipt of the reference in this Tribunal 
notices were issued to the Company and the Union 
and the notices were dulv served on both parties. 
The Company entered appearance in this 08809 
through its representative on 29th October 1960, 
the date for appearance fixed in the notices to the 
parties. But no appearance was made on behalf 
of the Union on that date. The notice to the Union 
waa found to have been duly served. The case was 
then adjourned to 12th November ۱1860 giving 
another chance to the Union to file its written 
statement, if any, and it was directed that in 
default of appearance by the Union on that date 
the 07৭6. was to be heard ex-parte. On that date 
also no appearahce was made on behalf of the 
Tnion and the case was taken up for ex-parte 
hearing at 1 p.m. 


At the ex-parte hearing, it was proved by the 
evidence produced on behalf of the Company that 
the workers concerned had already accepted 
different sums in full and final settlement of all 
their claims and dues against the Company afd 
the sume included salaries and atatutory leave pay 
up to 23rd April 1957. This has been proved by 
O.P.W. 1 Shri R. P. Choudhury, the Company’s 
Manager, and 71৭0 by the receipted vouchers of 
Ext. A series. This evidence coupled = with the 
non-appearance of the Union to press its claim 
on behalf of the workers concerned against the 
Company clearly establishes the position that none 
of these workers is entitled to any money from the 
Company besides the amount paid to him under 
the particular receipt of Ext. A series, by way of 
retrenchment compensation, and necessarily the 
claim made hy the Union on behalf of each of the 
workers as reflected in the issue framed must fail. 
O.P.W. 1 Shri R. P. Choudhury, has also testified 
that all disputes between the Company and the 
workers were fully and finally settled hy the pay- 
ments made to them upon the receipts of Fixt. A 
series. UWpon the facta proved at the hearing of 
the case IT am aatisfied that the 101) put forward 
by the Union on hehalf of the workers concerned 
is 2 correct and maintainable and hence it must 
ail. 


11) 1110 result I award that the claim made by 
the Union on behalf of the workers concerned 
against the Company in respect of retrenchment 


$922 THE CALCUITA GAZETTE, DECEMBER 15, 1960 


—— Soe লে 


compensation js not maintainable and the workers 
concerned are not entitled to any relief against the 
Company in this case. The case is disposed of 
accordingly by this ex-parte award.

T first take up the objection that the State

‘appropriate Government’’ has heen explained in 
section 2(a) of the Industrial Disputes Act. 
Clause (1) of section 2(a) indicates the circum- 
stances under which the Central Government is the 
“appropriate Government”? and lays down that 
that Government would be the “appropriate Gov- 
ernment’? in any caso of industrial dispute 
“concerning anv industry carried on by or under 
the authority of the Central Government or by a 
Railway Company or concerning any such controlled

Dated New Delhi, the 7th October 1960. 


No. 1-CA(3)/60.—In exercise of the powers 
conferred by sub-section (1) of section 30 of the 
Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 (XXXVIII of 
1949), the Council of the Institute of Chartered 
Accountants of India has made the following 
amendments in the Chartered Accountants Regula- 
tions, 1949, the same having heen previously pub- 
lished and approved by the Centra] Government as 
required under sub-section (3) of the said section. 


In the suid Regulations :— 
I. In Regulation 31B, add the following at the 
end :—— 


“Or (iii) a certificate from a surviving partner 
in Form ‘K-4’ or ‘K-G’ that the applicant 
has served either as an articled or as an 
audit clerk for the appropriate period, but 


is unable to produce a certificate in the . 


prescribed form signed by the chartered 
accountant with whom he served, by reason 
of the death or infirmity of the chartered 
accountant or for other sufficient cause.’’ 


II. In Regulation 42A, after sub-regulation 
(6) insert the following :— 


‘((5A) In the event of the death of the 
employer, his legal representative shall 
184116 10 the audit clerk a certificate in Form 
‘K-5'’ for the service rendered. Or in case 


the deceased employer was carrying on 
practice in partnership with another member 
of the Institute, the surviving partner shall 
issue to the audit clerk a cetrificate in Form 
‘K-6’ for the service rendered.”’ 


111. Change the heading of Chapter VIA as 
“Standing and other Committees’ instead of 
‘Standing Committees’. 


IV. After the existing Regulation 62G, insert 
the following :— 


**52-(44¢(1). -Committees other than Standing 
Committees: (i) Committees other than 
Standing Committees appointed by the 
Council under sub-section (2) of section 17 
of the Act, shall consist of wu Chairman, a 
Vice-Chairman and such other members of 
the Council as may be elected on it by the 
Council and any other members of the 
Institute who may be co-opted with the 
sanction of the Council. 


(ii) The Committees shall discharge such 
functions as may be decided by the Council 
from time to time. 


(iii) The provisions contained in Regulations 
62۸, 62B, 620, 62) and 62E relating to the 
lime and place of meetings, quorum, 
procedure for transaction of business, casting 
vote, minutes, etc., shal] ‘mutatis mutandis’ 
apply to such Committees except that the 
reterence to President and Vice-President 
in the above Regulations shall he construed 
as reference to Chairman and Vice-Chairma:. 
respectively of a Committee and the Secre- 
tary of the Counce)! shall be the Secretary 
for only such of the Committees as may he 


decided by the Council.

No. 3316-R/VITI-B-651/57.—In exercise of 
the powers conferred by section 99A of the Code 
of Crimina] Procedure (Act V of 1898), the Gov- 
ernor 18 pleased to declare the book in Urdu 
entitled ““Khak Aur Khoon” written by Nasim 
Hejazi, printed at the Ittehad Press and publish- 
ed by (QJuaini Kutubkhana, Lahore, and every copy 
of the said book and all other documents contain- 
ing copies, reprints and translations of or extracts 
from the said book forfeited to Government on the 
ground that the suid book contains matter, which 
in effect promotes feeling of enmity or hatred 
between different classes of citizens of India and the 
publication of which is punishable under section 
167۸ of the Indian Penal Code.

MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY 


Office of the Textile Commissioner 
(Powerlioom) 


Bombay, the 17th Noyember 1960. 
PRESS NOTE 


Unregistered looms—extension of time for 
application for permit. 


In the Press Note, issued by the Textile Com- 
missioner on Sth November 1960, owners of 
unregistered powerlooms working without permits 
issued under the Textile Control Orders were 
required to submit their applications hefore sUth 
November 1960. In view of several representations 
for extension of time, the Government of India 
are pleased to extend this period up to 4 
December 1960. 


2. In the form of application it was stated that 
upplications for سوک‎ should be accompanied by 
attested copies of Central Excise Licences. It will 
be sufficient if oa certificate is produced from the 
Central Excise authorities that the looms in ques- 
tion had been acquired and installed before 84 
October 1960, and have been issued licences under 
the Central Excise Rules.

ANNEXURE 


In the matter of an industrial dispute oxisting 
between Messrs. Harrisons and Crosfield Ltd., 
6 Church Lane, Calicutta-1, and their work- 
men represented by the 11817890175 and

BEFORE THE FOURTH INDUSTRIAL 
TRIBUNAL, WEST BENGAL 
Present: 


Shri K. K. MITRA, Judge, Fourth Industrial 
Tribunal. 


Shn 1). L. Sen Gupta, Advocate. 


For the Company: Shri 18. Goswami, an officer 
of Bengal Chamber of Commerce. 


For the Union: 


An industrial dispute between Messrs. Harrisons 
and Orosfield Limited (hereinafter referred to as 
the Company), 6 Church Lane, Calcutta-1, and 
their workmen represented by the Harrisons and 
Crostield (Caleutta) Employees’ Union (herein- 
after referred to as the Union), ۸ Krishna Laha 
Lane, Calcuttu-12, has been referred to this 
Tribunal for adjudication, over the following issue, 


by the Government of West Bengal, Labour 
Department, order No. 2347-I.R./IR/9L-55/59, 
dated the 13th May 1960. 

Issue 


Whether the dismissal of Shri Panchanan 
Bhattacharyya ia justified P To what relief, if aty, 
is he entitled P 


After service of usual notices upon the parties 
for appearance and for filing written statement, 
the Union filed its written statement on 20th June 
1960 After that the Company filed the written 
objection on 6th July 1960. 


AWARD 


The facts as disclosed in the pleadings, indicate 
that Shri Panchanun Bhattacherjee was a clerk 
employed by the Company for the last 14 years. 
He is a permanent resident of Joychandipur, P.S. 
Bishnupur in the district of 24-Parganas, situated 
at a distance of 21 miles from the oftice, and that 
he used to attend the office as a daily passenger. 
He used to come to Mominpur by bus and there- 
from either by tram car or Me bus. According to 
the version of the Union Shri Bhattacherjee was 
suddenly attacked with fever and bronchitis on

Under the proviso of section 03(2)(b) of the

It ×× turther urged by the employer that the pro-

The decision of the Industrial Tribunal, Bombay, 
108 the ease of Anthony (K.T.) and Messrs. Good 
Year Tyre and Rubber Co., of India (P) Ltd, 
Bombay, reported in 1958, L.L.J0., Vol. I, p. 877,

P) Ltd, Pathankot and their workmen, reported in

requisite of the exercise of the power of dismissal of 
the management, und the absence of the same would 
take the ease out of the mischief of section 33(2) of

Industrial Tribunal, Madras, in the case of Murug-

..L.3., Vol. I, p. 687. have carefully gone 
through these decisions and I hold that the absence 
of the Standing Orders does not confer a plenary 
power to the employer to proceed with the action in 
dismissing a workman arbitrarily. If there be 
Standing Orders, and the employer proceeds hona 
fide in accordance with the provisions of the Stand- 
ing Orders, the Tribunal would approve the action 
proposed to be taken by the employer in dismissing 
the workman for misconduct unconnected with the 
dispute. But if there ia no Standing Orders, the 
ban imposed under section 33(2) designed to secure 
status quo during the pendency of the proceedings 
before the Tribunal remains all the sume operative 
as against the employer. The employer cannot 
therefore take any advantage on the absence of 
Standing Orders which in) normal course should 
huve been maintained by this employer emploving 
more than 100 workmen in the industrial establish- 
ment,

But colourable exercise by the employer of his 
power to transfer a workman from one establish- 
ment of his at one place to another at a different 
place (e.g., when the transfer of a workman 1s 
ordered with a view to victimise him) can always 
he the subject of an industrial dispute, and can he 
the subject-matter of a complaint under section ۸ 
of the Act, if made without the previous permission 
of the Tribunal. Clearly, the order of transfer was 
passed with a view to punish the workman con- 
cerned for his trade union activities. There 1s 
nothing to show that the trade union activities 11) 
the matter of collecting subscriptions or otherwise 
was illegal. The action of the employer by trans- 
ferring the emplovee for auch activities and then 
dismissing the man for not carrying out such 
wrongful order cannot therefore be supported It 
is, therefore, directed that Razak Khan 709 سم‎ 
‘nstated to his old post at Jamgram Works and he 
he paid half of the 012] wages for the period of his 
unemployment. 


K. K. MITRA, 
Judge, Fourth Industrial Tribunal.

(Pear I 


By (Government order No, 4441-1.R./TR/10L- 
119/58, dated the 12th September 1959, the above 
industrial dispute was referred to this Tribunal 
under section 10 of the Tndustrial Disputes Act 
for adjudication of only issue, viz., ‘House rent 
allowance’. The Union filed written statement 
on 19th January 1960 and Messrs. Hindusthan 
Motors J.td., to he hereafter referred to as the 
Company, filed their written statement on 5th 
April 1960, The case was heard on 29th November 
1960 anf both parties examined one witness each 
and the argument was concluded on that date. 


The Company is an automobile industry started 
in 1942, but it actually commenced manufacture 
in 1949. At present if employs about 4,000 
workmen in ils automobile division besides several 
casual workers. The dispute relates to these 4,000 
workers. The Company has its factory at 
Witarpara in the district of Hooghly, and it has 
built certain quarters for the accommodation of its 
workmen. These quarters are let out to workmen 
on certain rates of rent per month. There is some 
difference in the evidence as to how many of its 
4,000 permanent workmen have heen accommodated 
in these quarters, the evidence of the Company’s 
Personnel Officer being that between 1,800 and 
2,000 permanent workmen have been so accomo- 
modated. The witness for the Union, however, 
stated that not more than 7) people had been 
allotted quarters, Te is not, however, expected to 
know the real position, und he admitted that the 
Personnel Officer of the Company who was in 
charge of allotment of quarters was in a position 
to give the correct figure. In the circumstances 
I accept the Company’s evidence on the point. The 
Company is also building new quarters and it is 
admitted on both sides that 96 new quarters are 
almost ready and would soon be allotted to work- 
men of the Company. I have also been assured 
by Shri বি. K. Rose. Counrel, on behalf of the 
Company that the Company has an intention to 
build more quarters so as to eventually accom- 
modnte all the wormen. 


Though the issue referred for adjudication 
relates to house rent allowance only, the written 
statement of the Tnion does not really contain any 
demand for such allowance. The TUhion’s 
grievances are that the workers are suffering badly 
for want of accommodation, that the rents charged 
bv the Company are high, that the Company does 
not ‘keep the quarters under proper repair and that 
the | sanitary and = water-supply — arrangements 
require improvement. The prayer in the written 
statement is that the Company should provide for 
free quarters for low paid workmen and should he 
directed to reduce the existing rates of rent by 
HO per cent. or grant suitable house rent allowance. 
Tt is also stated that the Company has been 
financially assisted hy the Central Government for 
the betterment of housing conditions and for 
building 800 rooms which it hus not yet done, and 
i prayer has been made that the Company should 
he directed to build more quartera. In his 
evidence the Assistant Secretary of the Tnion 
made further grievances that there waa no fixed 
procedure for allotment of aecommodation and that 
the management indulges in favouritism in the 
matter of allotment of quarters. 


Parr I] 


The above allegations and = grievances of the 
Union huve been dented by the Company and iti 
has also been demed that the Company has receiy ed 
any 110 from the Central Government for providnig 
housing accommodation to the workmen or tor 
building 800 rooms. Actually none ot the 
grievances detailed above fulls for consideration 
within the ambit of the issue refer:ed fol adjudica- 
tion. The issue simply is whether any house rent 
allowance should be provided and ھ‎ to that, as 
already stated. the Union has submitted nothing in 
its written statement and no case for house rent 
allowance has been made out by the evidence. The 
Company does not provide free quarters for any of 
its workmen so that a claim = for house rent 
allowance may be advanced on behalf of the work- 
01001) who are not so provided. The Company 
provides quarters and charges rent therefor, In 
the circumstances provision of quarters for some 
cannot be made a ground for claiming house rent 
allowance on behalf of the rest so long as they are 
not provided with quarters. According to the 

teyer in’ the Union’s written statement, the 
নি should be directed to reduce the existing 
rates of rent or grant suitable house rent allowance. 
this means that the claim for house rent allowanre 
has actually been made for those who have been 
provided with quarters on the alleged yround of 
high rates of rent charged from them. But the 
Union’s witness did not refer to the rates of rent ut 
all and did not even suggest that they were high. 
sy this ground also fails. No indication has also 
been given as to the kind of allowance claimed and 
no amount or standard has been mentioned either 
in the written statement of the Union or in the 
evidence of its witness. In the circumstances, the 
Uunion’s claim must naturally fail. 


In the case of Patna Electricity Supply Company, 
reported in 16 F.J.R. 210 the Supreme Court 
observed that housing accommodation of industrial 
labour is the primary responsibility of the State 
and that in the present economic condition of our 
industries it would he inexpedient 16 impose on the 
employers the obligation to provide housing 
aecommodation tor their employees. Tt was further 
observed that a scheme of wages properly fixed 
necessarily takes into account house rent amongst 
other relevant facts and that under a proper scheme 
of dearness allowance adjustments can be made 
when necessary from time to time so as to take 
info account an apprecinble rise in the rents which 
industrial labour may have to pay, So fur as the 
present industry 1s concerned. there has recently 
been an award by the present Tribunal to which the 
present Union was also n party. By that award 
which was published in the 54081011110, Gazette’ of 
June 28, 1960, it was found that the Company was 
no engineering industry and the award of the 
Third Major Engineering Tndustries Tribunal was 
enforced on it in fixing certain wage scales and 
dearness allowance. The said award of the Third 
Major Engineering Industries Tribual which was 
published in the “Calcutta Gazette, Extraordinary’’, 
dated November 4, 1958, shows that in fixing the 
minimum wages the cost of housing accommodation 
was also tuken into consideration. So when the 
workmen of this industry have beon awarded the 
minimum wages and dearness allowance a4 fixed 
hv the aforesaid award house rent should also be 
deemed to have been taken into account in arriv- 
sng at such rates of wages and dearness allowance. 


THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, DECEMBER 22, 1960 4()2 


There is no evidence that any engineering industry 
pays house rent allowance in addition to the rates 
of wages and dearness allowance, awarded by the 
Third Major Engineering Industries Tribunal, to 
apurt from the fact that the grievances mentioned 
in the written statement of the Union and in the 
evidence of the Union's witness are not relevant to 
the issue under reference, on the authority of the 
above decision of the Supreme Court the Tribunal, 
cannot impose on the Company an obligation to 
provide housing accommodation for all the 
employees. The Company has however, provided, 
as already stated, housing accommodation for 
nearly half of the employees and intends to extend 
accommodation further in future. That ought to 
have satisfied the grievances of the Union. Tho 
procedure for providing housing accommodation 
according to the length of service and priority of 
application for such accommodation رر‎ 1, 
followed by the Company, as staled by its Personnel 
Officer, cannot also be taken exception to. 1368৭110168, 
a large number of workmen are local people living 
in their homes nearby, and there is no suggestion 
that housing accommodation ia 1101 available to 
others who are not local people. The industry is 
not situated in Calcutta and there cannot be any 
diffeulty of housing accommodation in the region 
where the factory is situated. At least no evidence 
has been given to that effect. In the cirrumatances 
the claim of the Union must be 000] 19 hereby 
rejected,

viz., Butto Kristo Paul and Co, 14d. Employees’ 
Tnion is no longer in existence and contending 
that as such) this is not 01) industrial dispute. 
۸۱ the time of argument Shri K. .کا‎ ٥8) 
appearing for the company has argued that this is 
a case of retrenchment and as such is a matter 
apecified in the Third Schedule to the Industrial 
Disputes Act. So he has argued that this Court 
has no jurisdiction to adjudicate on this dispute. 


Findings 


T take up first the two preliminary objections 
raised by the company. As to whether this 
in n case of retrenchment, the order of reference 
does not say that this is a case of retrenchment. 
Neither the Union nor the company (× their 


. 


[Par] 


Ee 


respective written statements or in the evidence 
adduced by them respectively have said that this 
a cuse of retrenchment. Shri K. K. Maitra has 
drawn my attention to ‘paragraph 12 of صم‎ affi- 
davit, dated 1711) June 1960 of the Secretary of 
the Union, Therein the Secretary = says; 
“Kurther 1 say the lay-off and subsequent retrench- 
ment arc void as the company failed to pay the 
lay-off compensation as well as retrenchment com- 
pensation’. ‘The reading of the entire affidavit 
will make بد‎ clear that the Secretary of the Union 
does not adimit this to be a case of retrenchment. 
As no charge-sheet was issued to Shri Sailendra 
Nath Bose nor was any cauge shown for the ter- 
mination of his service, the Secretary of the Union 
guessed that this might be a case of retrenchment. 
So the sentence quoted by me above cannot be 
taken to be an admission on the part of the Union 
of this case being a case of retrenchment. More- 
over, there cun be no admission leading to 
estoppel on point of law. As to whether this is 
1 case of retrenchment or not will depend on the 
evidence adduced fhefore me about the merits of 
this case. As will appear when I discussed the 
evidence about the merits of the case, this is not 
n case of retrenchment. 


“As to the objection whether is is an industrial 
dispute, the company has produced a letter to the 
management purported to have been signed by 
90) employees of the company; therein they have 
stated that they are no longer members of the 
Union. lHven if this letter is taken to represent 
the true state of affair, it does not say that the 
signatories were not members of the Union at 
the crucial time, i.e., at the time when the dis- 
pute was raised, Even og to the present state of 
iffuir, O.P.W, 3 states even in his examination- 
in-chief that there are about 200 employees at 
the Head Office building of the company. So 
even now a majority of the employees of the com- 
pany are members of the Union, So I reject the 
objection of the company that this is not an indus- 
trial dispute. 


T now enter into the merits of the case. The 
main point in the case of, the company is that the 
management laid-off Shri Sailendra Nath Bose at 
his request; but thia sugyreation was not put to 
him when he was before me at the witness box. 
ال‎ in udmitted that the company is not an indus- 
trin] establishment but a commercial — establish- 
ment. So there is no provision for lay-off in such 
an establishment. So lay-off of employees in 
such an_ establishment is mala fide and even 
illegal. Hence even it be admitted that Shni 
Sailendra Nath Bose requested the management to 
lay him off, such a request cannot validate .an 
egal action. Further it is on evidence that 
Shri Sailendra Nath Bose was complaining to the 
Shops and Establishments Directorate against the 
company for non4apayment of his salary. Obvious- 
ly the company could not fake this in 6۹م‎ 
grace. So T hold that the laying-off of Shri 
Sailendra Nath Bose is only a trick played by the 
company on a helpless employee ignorant of the 
implications of law. There is also no evidence to 
show that Shri Sailendra Nath Bose stopped 
xigning the attendance register during the period 
of xo-called lay-off. Tf it 1s believed that he was 
laid off at his own 


request, it is not 
understood why he 


should stop = signing

of luy-off. So 1 believe the statement 
that one day towards the end of Ashar he was 
anked not to sign the attendance register. 41018 
18 virtually termination of his service. The com- 
pany has not tried to show any reason why his 
vervice hus been terminated, 


In view of the above considerations, ] hold that 
the lay-off followed by the termination of the 
wrvice of Shri Sailendra Nath Bose is unjustified. 
In view of what has transpired in evidence, 
specially, in view of the bad financial qwsition of 
the company I do not order his reinstatement. 
I order that the company sball pay him a com- 
pensation of Rs. 600 and all his arrear salary up 


to 14th March 1958. ‘This order shall take effect 
within a month of the publication of this award 
in the “Calcutta Gazette’.

THE FIRST SCHEDULE 


(See section 2) 


GENEVA CONVENIION FOR THE AMELIORATION OF THE CONDIMON 
OF TITE WOUNDED AND SICK ARMED FORCES IN THE FIELD 
or AuGusrt 12, 1949. 


The undersigned Plenipotentiaries of the Governments 
represented at the Diplomatic Conference held at (teneva 
from Apnml 21 to August 12, 1949, for the purpose of revising 
the Geneva Convention for the Relief of the Wounded and 
oe in Armies in the Field of July 27, 1929, have agreed as 
ollows : — 


CHAPTER I 


(}eNERAL PROVISIONS 


: Article 1 


The High Contracting Parties undertake to respect and 
to ensure respect for the present Convention in all circums- 
tances. 


Article 2 


In addition to the provisions which shall be implementud 
in peacetime, the present Conyentiou shall apply to all cases 
of declared war or of any other armed conflict which may 
arise between two or more of the 11181) Contracting Parties, 
even if the state of war is not recognized by one of thein. 


The Convention shall also apply to all cases of partial or 
total occupation of the territory of a High WUontracting 
Party, even if the said occupation meets with no armed 
resistance. 


Although one of the Powers in conflict may not be a party 
to the present Convention, the Powers who are parties there- 
to shalf remain bound by it in their mutual relations. They 
shall furthermore be bound by the Convention in relation 
to the said Power, if the latter accepts and applies the pro- 
visions thereof. 


Article 3 


In the case of armed conflict not of an international 
character occuring in the territory of one of the High Con- 
tracting Parties, each Party to the conflict shall he bound to 
apply, as a minimum, the following provisions: — 


(1) Persons taking no active part in the hostilities, in- 
cluding membors of armed forces who have Jaid 
down their orms and those placed hors de combat 
by sickness, wounds, detention, or any other 
caure, shall in all cireumstances be trented 
humanely, without any adverse distinction 
founded on race, colour, religion or faith, sex, 
birth or wealth, or any other similar criteria.

in peace time, the present Convention shall apply to all cases کت‎ one 
of declared war or of any other armed conflict which may gion,

thereof.

Artiote 4 


A. Prisoners of war, in the sense of the presenti 
Convention, are persons belonging to one of the following 
categories, who have fallen into the power of the enemy :— 


(1) Members of the armed forces of a Party to the 
conflict as well as members of militias or volunteer 
corps forming part of such armed forces, 


(2) Members of other militius and wembers of other 
volunteer corps, including those of organized 
resistance movements, belouging to a Party to the 
conflict and operating in or outside their own 
territory, even if this territory 1s occupied, 
provided that such militias or volunteer corps, 
including such organized resistance movements, 
fulfil the following conditions :— 


(a) that of being commanded by a person responsible 
for his subordinates; 


(b) that of having a fixed distinctive sign recognizable 
at a distance; 


(c) that of carrying arms openly; 


(d) that of conducting their operations in accordance 
with the laws and customs of war, 


(3) Members of regular armed forces who profess 
allegiance to a government or an authority not 
recognised hy the Detaining Power. 


(4) Persons who accompany the armed forces without 
actually being members thereof, such as civilian 
members of military aircraft crews, war corres- 
pondents, supply contractors, members of labour 
units or of services responsible for the welfare 
of the armed forces, provided that they have 
recelved atithorization from the armed forces 
which they accompany, who shall provide them 
for that purpose with an identity card similar to 
the annexed model. 


(6) Members of crews, including masters, pilota and 
apprentices, of the merchant marine and the crews 
of civil aircraft of the Parties to the conflict, who 
do not benefit hy more favourable treatment under 
any other provisions of international law. 


(6) Inhabitants of a non-occupied territory, who on the 
approach of the enemy spontaneotaly take up 
arms to resist the invading forces, without having 
had time to form themselves into regular armed 
units, provided they carry arms openly and 
respect the laws and customs of war.

Article 46 


The Detaining Power, when deciding upor the transfer

The transfer of prisoners of war shall always be effected

conditions to which the prisoners of war are accustomed

The Detaining Power shall supply prisoners of war

Article 47 


Sick or wounded prisoners of war shall 1100 be trana- 
ferred as long as their recovery may be endangered by the

Tf the combat zone draws closer to a camp, the prisoners 
of war in the said camp shall not be transfered unless theft 
transfer can be carried out in adequate conditions of safety, 
or unless they are exposed to greater risks by remaining on 
the spot than by being transferred. 


Article 48 


In the event of transfer, prisonera of war shall be 
officially advised of their departure and of their new postal 
address. Such notifications shall be given in time for them 
to pack their luggage and inform their next of kin. 


They shall be allowed to take with them their personal 
effects, and the correspondence nnd parcels whieh have 
arrived for them. The weight of such baggage may be 
limited, if the conditions of transfer so require, {o what 
each prisoner can reasonably earry, which shall in nO Case 
be more than twenty-five kilograms per head. 


Mail and parcels addressed to their former camp shall 
be forwarded to them without delay. The camp cominunder 
shall tuke, in agreement with the prisoners’ representative, 
uny measures needed to ensure the transport of the prisoners’ 
community property und of the luggage they are unable to 
take with them in consequence of restrictions imposed by 
virtue of the second paragraph of this Article. 


The costs of transfers shall be borne by the Detaining

Article 53 


The duration of the daily labour of prisoners of war, 
including the time of the journey to and fro, shall not be 
excessive, and must in no case exceed that permitted for 
civilian workers in the district, who are nationals cf the 
Detaining Power and employed on the same work, 


Prisoneta of war must be allowed, in the middle of the 
day’s work, a rest of not less than one hour. This rest will

Power are entitled, if the latter is of longer duration. They

cutive hours every week, preferably on Sunday or the day 
of rest in their country of origin. Furthermore, every 
prisoner who has worked for one yeur shall be granted a 
rest of eight consecutive days, during which his working 
pay shall be paid to him.

Prisoners of war who sustain accidents in connection

Article 5 


The fitness of prisoners of war for work shall be 
periodically verified by medical examinations, at 16886 once 
a mouth. The examinations shall have particular regard to 
تم‎ 70 of the work which prisoners of war are required 
to do. 


If any prisoner of war considers himself incapable of 
working, he shall be permitted {to appear before the medical 
authorities of his camp; Physicians or surgeons may 
recommend that the prisoners who are, in their opinion, 
unfit for work, be exempted therefrom. 


Article 56 


The organization and administration of labour detach- 
ments shall be similar to those of prisoner of war camps. 


Kvery labour detachment shall remain under the control 
of and administratively part of a prisoner of war camp. 
The military authorities and the commander of the said 
camp shall be responsible, under the direction of their 
government, tor the observance of the provisions of the 
present Convention in labour detachments. 


The camp commander shall keep an up-to-date record of 
the labour detachments dependent on his camp, and shall 
communicate it to the delegates of the Protecting Power 
of the International Committee of the Red Cross, or of other 
ogencies giving relief to prisoners of war, who may visit the 
camp.

tion

They shall furthermore be bound by the Convention in 
relation to the said Power, if the latter accepts and applies 
the provisions thereof.

Article 4 


Definition Persons protected by the Convention are those who, at a 

of protec- given moment and in any manner whatsoever, find them- 

ted persons selves, in case of a conflict or occupation, in the hands of a 
Party to the conflict or Occupying Power of which they are 
not nationals, 


Nationals of a State which is not bound by the Convention 
are not protected by it. Nationals of a neutral State who 
find themselves in the territory of a belligerent Slate, and 
nationals of a co-belligerent State, shall not be regarded ns

PART 1

Article 13 


The provisions of Part 11 cover the whole of the popula- 
tions of the countries in conflict, without any adverse 
distinction based, in particular, on race, nationality, religion 
or political opinion, and are intended to alleviate the 
sufferings caused by war. 


Article 14 


In time of peace, the High Contracting Parties and, 
after the outbreak of hostilities, the Parties thereto, may 
estublish in their own territory and, if the need arises, in 
occupied areas, hospital and safety zones and localities so 
organized as to protect from the effect of war, wounded, sick 
and aged persous, children under fifteen, expectant mothers 
and mothers of children under seven. 


Upon the outbreak and during the course of hostilities, 
the Parties concerned may conclude agreenrents on mutual 
recognition of the zones und localities they have created. 
They may for this purpose implement the provisions of the 
Draft Agreement annexed to the present Convention, with 
such amendments as they may consider necessary. 


The Protecting Powers and the International Committee 
of the Red Cross are invited to lend their good offices in order 
to facilitate the institution and recognition of these hospital 
and safety zones and localities. 


Article 16 


Any Party to the conflict may, either direct or through 
a neutral Eiate or some humanitarian organization, propose 
to the adverse arty to establish, in the regions where fighting 
is taking place, neutralized zones intended to shelter from 
the effects of war the following persons, without 
distinction : سے‎ 
(a) wounded and sick combatants or non-combatauts ; 


(b) civilian persons who take no part in hostilities, and 
who, while they reside in the zones, perform no 
work of a military character. 


When the Parties concerned have agreed upon the 
geographical position, administration, food supply and 
supervision of the proposed neutralized sone, a written ufiee- 
ment shall be concluded and signed by the representatives ol 
the Parties to the conflict. The agreement shall fix the 
beginning and the duration of the neutralization of the 
zone. 


Article 16 


The wounded and sick, us well os the infirm, and

As far as military considerations allow, each Party 10 the 
conflict shall facilitate the steps taken to search for the killed 
and wounded, to assist the shipwrecked and other persons 
exposed to grave danger, and to protect them against pillage 
and ill-treatment,

Article 18 


Civilian hospitals organized to give care to the wounded 
and = 911১, the infirm and maternity cases, may in no 
circumstances be the object of attack but shall at all times 
be reapected and protected by the Parties to the conflict. 


States which are Parties to a conflict shall provide all 
civilian hospitals with certificates showing that they are 
civilian hospitals and that the buildings which they occupy 
nre not used for any purpose which would deprive these 
hospitals of protection in accordance with Article 19, 


Civilian hospitals shall be marked by means of the 
emblem provided for in Article 38 of the Geneva Convention 
for the Amelioration of the Condition of the Wounded and 
Sick in Armed Forces in the Field of August 12, 1949, but 
only if so authorized by the State. 


The Parties to the conflict shall, in so far os military 
considerations permit, take the necessary steps to make the 
distinctive emblems indicating civilian hospitals clearly 
visible to the enemy land, air and naval forces in order to 
obviate the possibility of any hostile action, 


In view of the dangers 160) which hospitals may be exposed 
by being close to military objectives, it is recommended that 
such hospitals be situated as far as possible from such 
objectives. 


Article 19 


The protection to which civilian hospitals are entitled 
shall not cease unless they are used to commit, outside their 
humanitarian duties, acts harmful to the enemy. Protection 
may, however, cease only atter due warning has been given, 
hamiug, in all appropriate cases, a reasonable time limit, 
and after such warning has remained unheeded. 


The fuct that sick or wounded members of the armed 
forces are nursed in these hospitals, or the presence of small 
arms and ammunition taken from such combatants which have 
not yet been handed to the proper service, shall not be con- 
sidered to be acts harmful to the enemy. 


Article 20 


Persons regularly and solely engaged in the operation 
and administration of civilian hospitals, including the 
personnel engaged in the search for, removal and transport- 
ing of and caring tor wounded and sick civilians, the infirm 
and maternity cases shall be respected and protected. 


In occupied territory and in zones of military operations, 
the above personnel shall be recognisable by means of an 
identity catd certifying their status, bearing the photograph 
of the holder and embossed with the stamp of the responsible 
authority, and also by means of a stamped, water resistant 
armlet which they shall wear on the left arm while carryin 
out their duties. This armlet shall be issued by the State an 
shall bear the emblem provided for in Article 38 of the 
(teneva Convention for the Amelioration of the Condition of

August 12, 1949.

PART IIl 
STATUS AND TREATMENT OF PROTECTED PFRSONS 
SECTION I 


PROVISIONS COMMON TO THE TERRITORIES OF THE PARTIES TO 
THE CONFLICT AND TO OCCUPIED TERRITORIZS 


Articole 27 


Protected persons are entitled, in all circumstances, to 
respect for their persons, their honour, their family rights, 
their religious convictions and practices, and their manners 
and customs. They shall at oll times be humanely treated, 
and shall be protected especially against all acts of violence 
or threats thereof and against insults and public curiosity. 


Women shall be especially protected against any attack 
on their honour, in particular against rape, enforced prostitu- 
tion, or any form of indecent assault. 


Without prejudice to the provisions relating to their state 
of health, age and sex, all protected persons shall be treated 
with the same consideration by the Party to the conflict in 
whose power they are, without any adverse distinction based, 
in particular, on race, religion or political opinion. 


Iluwever, the Parties to the conflict may take such 
measures of control and security in regard to” protected 
Fersons as may be necessary as a result of the war. 


Article 28. 


The presence of a protected person may not be used to 
render certain points or areas immune from military opera- 
tions. 


Article 29 


The Party to the conflict in whose handa protected persons 
may be, is responsible for the treatment accorded to them by 
its agents, irrespective of any individual responsibility which 
may be incurred. 


Article 30 


Protected persons shall have every facility for making 
application to the Protecting Powers, fhe International 
Committee of the Red Cross, the National Red Cross (Red 
Jrescent, Red Lion and Sun) Society of the country where 
they may be, as well as to any organizations that might 
assist them. 


These several oryanizations shall be granted all facilities 
for that purpose by the authorities, within the bounds sct by 
military or security considerations. 


Apart from the visits of the delegates of the Protecting 
Powers and of the International Committee of the Red 
Cross, provided for by Article 143, thagDetaining or Occupy- 
ing Powers shall facilitate as much as possible visits to 
protected persons by the representatives of other organiza- 
tions whose object is to give spiritual aid or material relief 
to such persons. 


Article 31 


No physical or moral coercion shall be exercised 8468 
rrotected persons, in particular to obtain information from 
them or from third parties.

Article 32 


The 11181) Contracting Parties specifically agree that each 
of them is prohibited from taking any measure of such a 
character as to cause the physical suffering or extermination 
of protected persons in their hands. This prohibition applies 
not only to murder, torture, corporal punishment, 15 
and 17166110881] or scientific experiments not necessitated by the 
medical treatment of a protected person, but also to any other 
measures of brutality whether applied by civilian or military 
agents. 


Article 33 


No protected person may be punished for an offence he or 
she has not personally committed. Collective penalties and 
likewise all measures of intimidation or of terrorism are 
prohibited. 


Pillage is prohibited. 


Reprisals ayainst protected persons and their property are 
prohibited.

The taking of hostages 1s prohibited.

This provision shall in no way constitute an obstacle to 
the repatriation of protected persons, or to their return to 
their country of residenve after the cessation of hostilities. 


Protected persons may be transferred by the Detaining 
Power only to a Power which is a party ما‎ the present 
Convention and after the Detaining Power has 0 
self of the willingness and ability of such transferee Power 
to apply the present Convention. Jf protected persons are 
transferred under such circumstances, responsibility for the 
application of the present Convention rests on the Power 
accepting them, while they are in its custody. Neverthelass, 
if that Power fails to carry out the provisions of the present 
Convention in any important respect, the Power by which 
the protected persons were transferred shall, upon being so 
notified by the Protecting Power, take effective measures to 
correct the situation or shall request the return of the 
protected persons. Such request must be complied with. 


In no circumstances shall a protected person be trans- 
ferred to a country where he or she may have reason to fear 
مامت‎ for his or her political opinions or religious 
chiefs. 


The provisions of this Article do not constitute an obstacle 
to the extradition, in pursuance of extradition treaties 
concluded before the outbreak of hostilities, of protected

The Occupying Power shall not detain protected persons

so demand. 


The Occupying Power shall not deport or transfer parts 
of its own civilian population into the territory it occupies.

Protected persons who commit an offence which is

protected person unless the attention of the court has been 
particularly called to the fact that since the accused 1s not 
u national of the Occupying Power, he is not bound to it by 
any duty of allegiance. 

In any case, the death penalty may not be pronounced 
against a protected person who was under eighteen years of 
age at the time of the offence.

Article 87 


Canteens shall be installed in every place of internment,

CHAPTER X 


TRANSFERS OF 5 


Article 127 


The transfer of internees shall always be effected 
humanely. As a general rule, it shall be carmed out by rail 
or other means of transport, and under conditions at least 
equal to those obtaining for the forces of the Detaimin 
Power in their changes of station. If as an eee tin 
measure such removals have to be effected on foot, they may 
pot take place unless the internees are in a fit state of health, 
and may not in any case expose them to excessive fatigue. 


The Detaining Power shall supply internees during trans- 
fer with drinking water and food sufficient in uantity, 
quality and variety to maintain them in good health, and 
also with the necessary clothing, adequate shelter and the 
necessury medical attention. The Detaining Power shall 
take all suitable precautions to ensure their safety during 
transfer, and shall establish before their departure a com- 
plete list of all internees transferred. 


Sick, wounded or infirm internees and routernity cases 
shall not be transferred if the journey would be seriously 
detrimental to them, unless their safety imperatively so 
demands. 


Tf the combat zone draws close to a place of internment, 
the internees in the said place shall not be transferred unless 
their removal can be carried out in adequate conditions of 
safety, or unless they are exposed to greater risks by remain- 
ing on the spot than by being transferred. 


When making decisions regarding the transfer of inter- 
nees, the Detaining Power shall take their interests into 
account and, in particular, shall not do anything to پ7۶‎ 
the difficulties gf repatriating them or returning them ta 
their own homes.

Article 146 


The High Contracting Tarties undertake to enact any 
legislation necessary to provide effective penal sanctions for 
persons committing, or ordering to be committed, any of the 
grave breaches of the present Convention defined in the 
followmg Article. 


Each High Contracting Party shall be under the obliga- 
tion to search for persons alleged to have committed, or to 
have ordered to be committed, such grave breaches, and shall 
bring such persons, regardless of their nationality, before ita 
own courts. It may also, if it prefers, and in accordance with 
the provisions of its own legislation, hand such persons over 
for trial to another High Contracting Party concerned, 
wrovided such High Contracting Party has made out a prima 
acie case, 


Each High Contracting Party shal] take measures neces- 
sary for the suppression of all acts contrary to the provisions 
of the present Convention other than the grave breaches 
defined in the following Article. 


In all circumstances, the accused persons shall benefit 
by safeguards of proper trial and defence which shall not be 
less favourable than those provided by Article 105 and those 
following of the Geneva Convention relative to the Treatment 
of Prisoners of War of August 12, 1949. 


Article 147 


Grave breaches to which the preceding Article relates 
shall be those involving any of the following acts, if com- 
mitted against persons or property protected by the present 
Convention: wilful killing, torture or inhuman treatment, 
including biological experiments, wilfully causing great 
suffering or serious injury to body or health, unlawful 
deportation or transfer or unlawful confinement of a protected 
person, compelling a protected person to serve in the forces 
of a hostile Power, or wilfully depriving a protected person 
of the rights of fair and regular trial prescribed in the 
present Convention, taking of hostages and extensive destruc- 
tion and appropriation of property, not justified by military 
necessity and carried out unlawfully and wantonly. 


Article 148 


No High Contracting Party shall be allowed to absolve 
itself or any other High Contracting Party of any liability 
incurred by itself or by another High Contracting Party in 
respect of کا سس‎ referred to in the preceding Article. 


Article 149 


At the request of a Party to the conflict, an enquiry shall 
be instituted, in a manner to be decided between’ the 
interested Parties, concerning any alleged violation of the 
Convention. 


If agreement has not been reached concerning the pro- 
cedure for the enquiry, the Parties should agree on the choice 
of an umpire who wil] decide upon the procedure to be 
followed. 


Once the violation has been established, the Parties to the 
conflict shall put an end to it and shall repress it with the 
least. possible delay.

SECTION II 
FINAL PROVISIONS 


Article 150 


The present Convention is established in English and in 
French. Both texts are equally authentic. 


_ The Swiss Federal Council shall arrange for official transla- 
tions of the Convention to be made in the Russian and 
Spanish languages. 


Article 151 


_ The present Convention, which bears the date of this day, 
is open to signature until February 12, 1950, in the name of 
the Powers represented at the Conference which opened اج‎ 
Geneva on April 21, 1949. 


Article 1h2 


The present (Convention shall be ratified a» soon as possible 
and the ratifications shal] be deposited at Berne. 


A record shall be drawn up of the deposit of each instru- 
ment of ratification and certified copies of this record shall 
be transmitted by the Swiss Federal Council to all the Powers 
in whose name the Convention has been sigued, or 6 
accession has been notified. 


Article 158 


The present Convention shal] come into force six months 
nfter not less than two instruments of ratification have been 


deposited. 


Thereafter, it shall come into force for each , High 
Contracting Party six months after the deposit of the instru- 
ment of ratification. 


Article 154 


In the relations between the Powers who are bound hy the 
Hague Conventions repecting the Jaws and Customs of War 
on Land, whether that of July 29, 1899, or that of October, 
18, 1907, and who are parties to the present Convention, this 
last Convention shall be supplementary to Sections II and 
111 of the Regulations annexed to the abovementioned 


Conventions of the Hague. 
Article 165 


From the date of its coming into force, i1 shall be open 
to any Power in whose name the present Convention has not 
been signed, to accede to this Convention. 


Article 156 


Accessions shal] he notified in writing to the Swiss 
Federal Council, and shall take effect six months after the 
date on which they are received. 


The Swiss Federal Council shall communicate the acces- 
sions to all the Powers in whose name the Convention has been 
signed, or whose accession has heen notified. 


Article 157 


The situations provided for in Articles 2 and 3 shall give 
immediate eftect to ratifications deposited and accessions 
notified by the Parties to the conflict before or after the 
beginning of hostilities or occupation. ‘The Swiss Federal 
Council shall communicate by the quickest method any 
ratifications or accessions received from Parties to the conflict.

Article 158 


Kach of the High Contracting Parties shall be at liberty Donna fia: 
tv denounce the present Convention. 


The denunciation shall be notified in writing to the Swies 
Federal Council, which shall transmit it to the Governments 
of all the High Contracting Parties. 


The denunciation shall take effect one year after the 
notification thereof has been made to the Swiss Federal 
Council. However, a denunciation of which notification has 
been made at a time when the denouncing Power is involved 
in a conflict shall not take effect until peace has been 
concluded, and until after operations connected with release, 
repatriation and re-establishment of the persons protected by 
the present Convention have heen terminated. 


The denunciation shall have effect only in respect of the 
denouncing Power. 1+ shall in no way impair the obligations 
which the Parties to the conflict shall remain bound to fulfil 
by virtue of the principles of the law of nations, as they 
result from the usages established among civilized peoples, 
from the laws of humanity and the dictates of the public 
conscience, 


Article 159 


The Swiss Federal Council shall register the present Registra- 
Convention with the Secretariat of the United Nations. Ter with 
The Swiss Federal Council shall also inform the Secre- اس ا‎ 
tariat of the United Nations of all ratifications, accessions 
and denunciationa received by it with respect to the present 


Convention.

deposited in the Archives of the Swiss Confederation. The

ANNEXURE 


In the matter of an industrial dispute between 
Messrs. Purulia Electric Supply Corporation 
Ltd., Purulia, and their workers represented 
by the Purulia Electric Supply Workers’ 
Union, Nilkuthidanga, P.O. Purulia. (Case

BEFORE THE SKCOND LABOUR COURT, 
WEST BENGAT, 


Present: 


Shri HEM RANJAN DEB, Presiding Officer,

Appearances: 


For the Company: Shri S. K. Bhattacharjee, an 
ofheiral of the Association of Manufacturers, 
Commercial and Traders, ussisted by Shri 
8 13. Ghosh, Director and Dr. T. P. Rai,

Ry order No. 47677 R./TR/10L-9/57, dated 
Caleutta, the 15th November 1958, Government 
of West Bengal, Labour Department, referred an 
industrial dispute between Messrs. Purulia 
Klectric Supply Corporation Jitd., Purulia, and 
their workers represented by the Purulia Flectric 
Supply Workers’ Tnion to the Second Labour 
Court) for adjudication regarding the issues 
mentioned in the order of reference. 


(1) Revision of pay scales, grades and (۸۰ 
of the different categories of the monthly 
paid workmen. 


(2) Revision of wages of and provision of ۸ 
to the daily-rated workers. 


(3) Provision for gratuity for all categories of 
workmen. 


The Purulia Electrie Supply Workers’ Union 
(hereinafter referred to aa the Union), has stated 
in its written statement that Messrs. Purulin 
Electric Supply Corporation 1۸8. (hereinafter 
referred to as the Company), are a prosperous con- 
cern and that particularly since 3rd April 45 
the Company has been earning heavy revenues 
from yeur to vear. The Union has stated in its 
written statement the minimum monthly wages of 
n worker in different Electric Supply Companies 
and by comparison has pointed out that the 
minimum monthly wage of a worker of the above 
Companv is fur below that in the other companies. 
So the Thion has stated its claim as regarda the 
three issues mentioned in the order of reference 
Tt hna atated pav 90,01৭ grades and = dearness 
allowance of the different categories of the 


[Pari ] 


monthly-paid workmen and daily-rated workers of 
the Company which it claims. It has also claimed 
for provision of gratuity ata rate of 16 0855 
wages for every completed year of service. 


The Company, on the other hand, has contended 
that it suffered heavy losses from its inception رر‎ 
1940 up to the year 1955. After that year it has 
made some profits, but atill the outstanding losses 
are very heavy. In the year 1949 the Company 
was forced to take a loan of Rs. 3 Inkha from the 
Industrial Finance Corporation’ of India. So the 
financial position of the Company 28 none but 
satisfactory. The companies to which the Union 
has referred in its written statement are big and 
prosperous eoneerna and compurison 01 this 
Company with those companies is out of place. 
Since 1955 the Company has been giving a number 
of monetary and other benefits to its employees 
which were not in existence prior to 1955. The 
Company contends that it is unable to give further 
and to revise upward the salaries and wages of 
its employees, not to speak of granting the scales 
of pay and dearness allowance demanded by the 
Union in its written statement. 


Findings 


The legal 1epresentative of the Company in his 
cross-examination of P.W, 1, the General Secre- 
tury of the Union, has made much of the fact 
that the Company is not a generating Company, 
wWherens some of the companies with which 
comparison has been made by the Union are 
generating ones. But such an argument does not 
lie in his mouth, because the case of the Company 
is that it has heen making profits after it stopped 
generating electric energy and began to purchase it 
from the D.V.C Whatever may be said about 
the companies which have been compared with 
this Company by the Union, it must be said that 
Burdwan Electric Supply Company stands almost 
at a par with this Company in that both of them 
purchase electricity from the D.V.C. and I can 
certainly presume that they have been purchasing 
electricity at the same price. I have also consi- 
dered the awards of some of the Tribunals 8 
respect of some Eleetric Supply Companies in the 
mofussil towns of West Bengal, this can be easily 
compared with the present Company 


But this comparison is not enough. Before I 
can saddle the Company with any extra financial 
liability, T shall have to be sure that the Company 
ia capable of bearing that burden. It is admitted 
by the Company that though it was making losses 
up to 1955, its profits have been rising 
continuously since that year. In the year ending 
on 9181 March 1958, the Company made a clear 
profit of a little over Ra. 33,000, vide Statutory 
Accounts (Ext ©). This shows that the former 
losses have been completely recouped. It is also 
seen from the statements of accounts for different 
vears that the Company has eheen liquidating its 
debts There is another factor: the Company 
has, amongst its assets, plants and machineries. 
Obviously those plants and machineries were pur- 
chased for generating electricity. So the 
Company no longer requires them. It is no 
evidence adduced on behalf of the Company that 
the Company is trying to sell them and has 


Part 1] 


incurred an expenditure of a_ little over 
Ra. 16,000 for overhauling of the generating sets 
১৭) the sale-proceeds ot the generating sets wil] be 
a sort of wind-fall income to the Company. In 
view of the above considerations, it cannot be held 
that the present financial condition of the Com- 
pany or its future prospect is bad. So I reject 
the contention of the Company that it is unable 
to bear the financial burden of any upward 
revision of the wage and salaries of its টি 
whatsoever, 


It is clear from evidence that while the scale 
of pay of the Accountant is Rs, 80—5—1380, that 
of the Tlead Clerk is Ra. 60—5—125. It 18 not 
understood why the Company which can afford to 
pay 115 Accountant a scale of pay from Re. 80 to 
Rs. 180 cannot pay a higher scale to the Head 
(Clerk. Again the Company pays the old Assist- 
ant Meter Reader in the scale of Ra. 30—2—A0, 
whereas it haus given an initial pay of Rea. 45 per 
month to a newly appointed Assistant Meter 
Reader. All this show that the Company has 
paid better saluries to some of its employees. As 
T have discussed ahove, the Company has the 
financial capability to pay better salaries and 
wages to all its employees. 


In consideration of the present and future 
financial capacity of the Company and of the 
scales of pay paid by the sister concerns, I decide 
the isaues mentioned in the order of reference as 
follows :— 


I order that the scales of pay of the different 
categories of employees should be revised as 
follows : سس‎ 

(1) Head Clerk—Rs. 90-—-6—150. 


(2) Cashier, Bill Clerk, Despatch Clerk and 
Storekeeper—Rs. 60—4—100. 


(8) Jineman and Meter Reader—Rs. 54b—3— 
85 


(4) Assistant Meter Reader and Blacksmith-— 
Rs. 45—2—b. 


The above scales of pay shall take effect from ۲۷ 
January 1961, on which date the incumbents of 
the above categories shall get the next increment 
in the new scales of pay irrespective of the dates 
on which their increments would otherwise fall 
due. The pay of the Assistant Meter Readers on 
Ist January 1961 shall, however, be fixed at the 
stage of the new seale which they would have 
reached had they started service at the initial pay 
of the present acale with half the period of service 
actually put in by them, 


The scales of pay of the other categories of 
monthly-paid employees would remain unchanged. 


e 

The financial condition of the Company is not 
ند“‎ good aa to allow any further inerease in dear- 
ness allowance. So the present rate of dearness 
allowance at 25 per cent. of the pay should 
continue, ; 

Issue No, 2: The Union has failed to make out 
any case for revision of the wages of the daily- 
rated workers. So T do not order any revision of 
the wages of the daily-rated workers. I, how-

As to the seeond issue, the case of the Union,

The company in its written statement has raised 
a preliminary objection that Messrs. Kharibari 
Tea Estate mentioned as a party in the order of 
reference is not a person but a property, wd tliat 
ay such it cannot ۶ made a party in any adjudi-

which owns and possesses Kharibari Tea Escate be 
brought on record, Though technically speaking, 
this contention of the company is correct, this can- 
not affect the validity of the order of reference. 
The main purpose of the order of reference, is for 
adjudication on oan industrial dispute which 
has arisen, and the main purpose of any 


adjudication thereon should be to promote 
industrial peace. Adjudiention of indus- 
trial dispute should not he — thwarted 


by the niceties of legal technicalities. In the 
present case Kharibari Tea Company 15111716961 has 
put in appearance and has contested the oase 
throughout. Further the order of reference nen- 
tions Messrs. Kharibari Tea Estate aa one of the 
parties, meaning obviously Messrs. Kharibari Tea

any doubt as to who are the parties in the present 
dispute. Hence 1 reject the preliminary objec- 
tion of the company and proceed to adjudicate on 
the second issue in the order of reference.

Decision 

Though the company hus narrated a number of 
incidents in which Shri Kastu Routia was involved 
in the past, they are immaterial for adjudication 
on the present dismissal of Shri Kastu Routia, os 
the company dismissed him on the  charge-sheet 
about the incidents of 30th January 1957, 31st 
January 1957 and Ist February 1957. So the point 
for my determination would be whether his dia- 
missal on the above charge-sheet is justified. The 
Union denies that any enquiry was held. The 
compuny contends that proper enquiries were held. 
The company has adduced evidence in support of 
the fact that an enquiry about the charge-sheet 
was held. The documentary evidence about — the 
enquiry are three sheets of paper alleged to he 
statements of three witnesses, none of.them has 
been produced before me. It is on the evidence 
of the company that the statements of other 
witnesses were recorded at the enquiry; but no 
such statement has been produced before me. ‘The 
company contends that Shri سام کا‎ Routia was 
present at the enquiry, but the company has not 
produced any documentary evidence in support of 
its contention. The oral evidence রাকা Ly the 
company also leads to the inference that the 
presence of Shri Kastu  Routia at the alleged 
enquiry is doubtful, and that if he was at all 
present at the enquiry, he was not given «ample 
opportunity to defend himself. There is also 
nothing on record to show when and how the 
enquiry was held. So I am unable to hold that 
any enquiry, not to speak of a proper enquiry, was 
held about the charge-sheet issued to Shri Naatu 
Routin. Hence the whole case about his dismissal 
is at large before me. 


The company has adduced ‘evidence about the 
incidents of 80th January 1957, 9181 January 1957 
and Ist February 1957. There is no reason to dis- 
believe that evidence. Particularly, the  vidence 
na to the incident on Ist February 1957 when Shri 
Kastu Routia is alleged to bave assaulted Shri 
Bhuleswar Kumbhakar is very convincing. 11

ANNEXURE 
In ‘the matter of a complaint under section 33A 
of the Industrial Disputes Act, filed by 
Shri Buniadi Ram, an employee of Messrs. 
Chungking Dyors and Dry Cleaners, 3 Harring- 


ton Street, represented by the Laundry 
Workers’ Union against the aforesaid 
company. (Case No. 63/33A /1959.) 


BEFORE THE SECOND LABOUR COURT, 
WEST BENGAL 


Present: 
Shri 11150 RANJAN DEB, Presiding Officer, 
Second Labour Court. 


Appearances : 
For the Company: Shri S. C. Seu, Advocate. 


Kor the complainant: Shn .لزا‎ K. Nandi, 
Advocate. 


The original reference out of which the present 
complaint under section 394 of the পাহারা 
Disputes Act has arison was made under Govern- 
ment order No. 8U6-I.R./1R/11L-27/59, dated 2nd 
March 1909. 


The case of the complainant Shri Buniadi ۰۱ 
is that the compuny deprived him of the housinyg 
accommodation on 5th October 1959 and as such 
violated the provision of section 33 of the Industrial 
Disputes Act. 


Shri 8. C. Sen, Advocate, appeuring for the 
company has raised the preliminary objection that 
this ig not a violation of section 33 of the Industrial 


4096 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, DECEMBER 29, 1960 


Disputes Act, and as such this complaint under 
seation 383A of the Industrial Disputes Act is not 
maintainable. 


Findings 


Section 33(2)(a) says that during the 175 
of a proceeding an employer may alter the 
conditions of service applicable to a worker in any 
matter not connected with the dispute. In the 
present case it is not the case of the complainant 
that provision of housing ucvommodation is in any 
way connected with the dispute raised in the 
original order of reference. So section 33(2) (a) 
clearly empowers the employer in this case to 
change the condition of service relating to housing 
accommodation of Shri Buniadi Ram. The only 
point raised by Shri P. K. Nandi, Advocate, 
appearing for the complainant, is that in the 
present 0889 the company changed the condition of 
service not in accordance with the atanding orders. 
But it is admitted that this company has no 
standing orders. So the question arises whether 
in view of the absence of any standing orders the 
company is precluded from exercising the power 
given to it under section 338(2)(a). Having regard 
to the scheme of provisions of the amended 


Industrial Disputes Act and to the provisions of 
section 38 in the Aot of 1947, I hold that the 
absence of stunding orders, does not preclude an 
employer from exercising the power conferred by 
section 33(2)(a) of the amended Industrial 
10181906685 Act. So I hold that the company did 
not violate section 33 of the Industrial Disputes 
Act by depriving Shri Buniadi Ram of the housing 
acoommodation. Hence the present complaint 
under section 338A of the Industrial Disputes Act 
is not maintainable. 


Dictated and corrected by me.
